description: How linear and binary search algorithms work, traced step by step on small datasets.
content_html:
Why Searching Matters

Searching is one of the most fundamental operations in computing. Every time you look up a contact on your phone, query a database, or ask a search engine a question, a search algorithm is running in the background. Your exam covers two searching algorithms: linear search and binary search. Understanding when to use each one, and being able to trace them by hand, are core exam skills.

Linear Search

Linear search (also called sequential search) is the simplest possible search algorithm. It checks each item in the list from the first to the last, one at a time, until it either finds the target or runs out of items. It works on any list — sorted or unsorted.

Below is a linear search in pseudocode. It searches a list called names for the value stored in target:

SET found = FALSE
SET i = 0
WHILE i < LENGTH(names) AND found = FALSE
  IF names[i] = target THEN
    SET found = TRUE
    OUTPUT “Found at position ” & i
  END IF
  SET i = i + 1
END WHILE
IF found = FALSE THEN
  OUTPUT “Not found”
END IF
Key Fact

Linear search may check every item in the list in the worst case — if the target is last or not present at all. For a list of n items, the worst case is n comparisons. Binary search, by halving the list each time, needs at most \ (\log_2 n \) comparisons.

List: [3, 7, 12, 5, 9]. Target: 12.

StepIndex checkedValueMatch?
103No
217No
3212Yes — found!

The algorithm stops after three comparisons. If the target were 99 (not in the list), it would check all five items before reporting “Not found.”

Binary Search

Binary search is much faster than linear search on large lists, but it has one critical requirement: the list must be sorted before binary search can be applied. Binary search works by repeatedly halving the search space. It finds the middle item, compares it to the target, and discards the half of the list that cannot contain the target.

Here is the binary search algorithm in pseudocode:

SET low = 0
SET high = LENGTH(list) - 1
SET found = FALSE
WHILE low <= high AND found = FALSE
  SET mid = (low + high) DIV 2
  IF list[mid] = target THEN
    OUTPUT “Found at position ” & mid
    SET found = TRUE
  ELSE IF target < list[mid] THEN
    SET high = mid - 1
  ELSE
    SET low = mid + 1
  END IF
END WHILE
IF found = FALSE THEN
  OUTPUT “Not found”
END IF
Key Fact

Binary search requires the list to be sorted in ascending (or descending) order. Without sorting, comparing the midpoint to the target gives no information about which half of the list to discard, so the halving strategy breaks down entirely.

Sorted list (indices 0–6): [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38]. Target: 23.

Passlowhighmidlist[mid]Action
10631223 > 12 → low = 4
246523Match! Found at index 5

Only two comparisons were needed to find the target in a list of seven items. A linear search would have needed six comparisons to reach index 5.

Comparing Linear and Binary Search

The table below summarises the key differences. In exam “compare” questions, you must make explicit contrasts — say “unlike linear search…” rather than describing each in a separate paragraph.

FeatureLinear searchBinary search
List must be sorted?NoYes
Worst-case comparisons (n items)nlog₂n
Best-case comparisons1 (target is first)1 (target is midpoint)
Works on small lists?Yes — often simplerYes, but overhead of sorting may not be worth it
Works on large lists?Slow — may check millions of itemsFast — 30 comparisons suffices for 1 billion items

Choosing Between Linear and Binary Search

The right algorithm depends entirely on two questions: is the list already sorted, and how often will you search it? If the data arrives in arbitrary order and only needs to be searched once, the cost of sorting first is wasted, so a linear search wins. If the same dataset is searched repeatedly, the one-off sorting cost is paid back many times over because every subsequent binary search runs in logarithmic time. Long-lived data structures — phone books, dictionaries, sorted database indexes — are designed around this trade-off.

Binary search also assumes the data lives in a structure that supports random access, where any index can be inspected in constant time. Arrays satisfy this requirement, but linked lists do not — reaching the middle of a linked list itself takes linear time, which cancels the algorithm’s headline advantage. When the spec asks why binary search is unsuitable in a particular scenario, an answer that mentions either “the data is unsorted” or “the structure does not allow random access” will earn the mark.
exam_tip_html: In “compare” questions about search algorithms, always make explicit contrasts — “unlike linear search, which can work on unsorted lists, binary search requires the list to be sorted.” State a concrete advantage for each direction of comparison. For trace-table questions on searching, show every pass: record the values of low, high and mid after each iteration, not just the final answer. Missing rows cost marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Linear search checks each item in order from the start; it works on unsorted lists but is slow for large datasets, with up to n comparisons in the worst case.
  • Binary search halves the search space each time, needing at most log₂n comparisons — but the list must be sorted first.
  • For small or unsorted lists, linear search is simpler; for large sorted datasets, binary search is far more efficient.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a requirement for binary search but NOT for linear search?
A) The list must contain integers only
B) The list must be sorted
C) The list must have an odd number of items
D) The list must be stored in a 2D array
practice_questions.marks: B) The list must be sorted [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the maximum number of comparisons needed to search a sorted list of 8 items using binary search.
practice_questions.marks: 3 comparisons [1 mark] (since log₂ 8 = 3). Accept 4 if working shown with rounding up.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of binary search compared to linear search.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantage: Binary search is much faster on large sorted lists / at most log₂n comparisons vs up to n for linear search [1 + 1 for development].
Disadvantage: Binary search requires the list to be sorted first / if the list changes frequently, re-sorting adds overhead [1 + 1 for development].
Mastering: Both points with development and explicit comparison.
Secure: Both points, one developed.
Developing: One point with development.
Emerging: One valid point.

practice_questions.text: Write a pseudocode algorithm for a linear search that searches a list called 'scores' (with 10 items, indices 0 to 9) for a target value entered by the user. Output the index if found or 'Not found' if not.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: RECEIVE target, initialise found/index, correct WHILE loop checking index < 10 AND found = FALSE, IF comparison inside loop, set found = TRUE and output index, post-loop check for not found — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Logic correct, minor issue with loop boundary or keyword — 3-4 marks.
Developing: Loop and IF present but incomplete — 2 marks.
Emerging: RECEIVE and some loop structure — 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: A school database of 50,000 student records is searched frequently. The records are sorted alphabetically by surname. Discuss whether binary search or linear search would be more suitable, justifying your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues binary search is suitable (sorted list meets prerequisite, log₂ 50000 ≈ 16 comparisons vs up to 50000 for linear), develops with efficiency argument, acknowledges linear search as simpler to implement / suitable for unsorted data, reaches a justified conclusion that binary search is preferable for a large, already-sorted dataset.
Secure: Binary search recommended with efficiency justification and acknowledgement of at least one trade-off.
Developing: Correct recommendation, basic efficiency point, limited development.
Emerging: Identifies binary search as faster without justification.

flashcard_questions.a: The list must be sorted in ascending or descending order.

After comparing the midpoint and finding the target is larger, what changes in binary search?
flashcard_questions.a: The low pointer moves to mid + 1, discarding the lower half.

flashcard_questions.q: When is linear search preferred over binary search?
flashcard_questions.a: When the list is small, unsorted, or changes frequently so re-sorting is costly.

glossary_terms.definition: A search algorithm that checks every item in a list one by one from the start until the target is found or the list ends.
A search algorithm that repeatedly halves a sorted list to home in on the target item, requiring the list to be sorted first.
An algorithmic time complexity that grows in proportion to the logarithm of the input size, meaning a doubling of input size adds only one extra step.
